claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Ab initio and molecular-dynamics calculations are too computationally demanding for efficient high-throughput alloy screening.
CALPHAD can require substantial computing resources and can be limited by incomplete databases for high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning models have previously been used to predict Young's modulus, yield stress, and toughness-related properties of alloys.
Existing approaches have difficulty capturing fracture behavior in highly heterogeneous HfNbTiVAl10.
A single surrogate pipeline can combine filtered ab initio data on local composition and lattice strain with grain-boundary, dislocation-density, and other microstructure-resolved descriptors.
The proposed physics-informed neural-network workflow can accurately predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture loading.
Descriptors of local chemical inhomogeneity, grain-boundary character, and dislocation barriers adequately represent the mechanically relevant hierarchical microstructure.
Localized composition and strain data allow the model to account for atomic-scale interactions affecting dislocation behavior and crack-tip processes.
Lattice distortion and heterogeneous slip pathways jointly control stiffness, yielding, and energy absorption in this alloy.
The proposed workflow will improve property-prediction accuracy by 20–30% relative to coarse-grained thermophysical or purely empirical machine-learning approaches.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost and execution time by 50–70% relative to the prior approaches.
The workflow is intended to apply during room-temperature and elevated-temperature uniaxial tensile and standardized fracture testing of HfNbTiVAl10 with varied subgrain morphologies.
Prediction reliability will diminish when composition or hierarchical microstructure lies substantially outside the training domain.
Unmodeled secondary phases, markedly different lattice parameters, or new chemical additions are examples of changes likely to make the model unreliable.
Sparse high-fidelity data on microstructural heterogeneities and fracture-critical flaws may limit extrapolation to new compositions or morphologies.
The hypothesis is falsified if any one of Young's modulus, yield strength, or fracture toughness differs from prediction by more than 10% for at least half of the blinded test samples.
